subject: ss-medical-oncology
title: Testicular Seminoma Staging, Post-Chemo Masses, Teratoma and Choriocarcinoma

steps.tx: Following radical inguinal orchiectomy, node-positive **testicular seminoma** is categorized as Stage IIA (retroperitoneal lymph nodes two centimetres or less) or Stage IIB (nodes measuring two to five centimetres). Primary retroperitoneal lymph node dissection (RPLND) is contraindicated in seminoma because of exquisite radiosensitivity and chemosensitivity. While dog-leg radiotherapy remains an alternative for Stage IIA, systemic **cisplatin-based chemotherapy** (etoposide plus cisplatin for four cycles, or BEP for three cycles) is the preferred standard for Stage IIB disease.
steps.say: When you manage a patient with stage two testicular seminoma, your first principle is that primary surgical lymphadenectomy plays no role. Pure seminoma is exquisitely sensitive to both radiation and chemotherapy. While external beam radiation to the para-aortic and ipsilateral iliac nodes is acceptable for stage two A, standard multi-agent chemotherapy using either four cycles of EP or three cycles of BEP is preferred for stage two B nodal disease.

steps.tx: Residual masses after chemotherapy for pure seminoma consist predominantly of dense fibrous tissue or necrosis rather than viable cancer. For any **residual mass** measuring less than three centimetres on computed tomography, active surveillance is recommended regardless of functional imaging. If a residual mass measures **three centimetres or greater**, **FDG-PET/CT** must be performed at least six weeks (optimally twelve weeks) after chemotherapy completion. A PET-negative scan warrants close observation, whereas PET avidity warrants surgical biopsy or resection.
steps.say: Interpreting post-chemotherapy residual retroperitoneal masses in seminoma requires careful adherence to size thresholds and timing rules. Small masses under three centimetres contain inactive necrotic scar tissue in over ninety percent of cases, so you simply observe them. When a residual mass measures three centimetres or larger, obtain an FDG-PET scan at least six weeks after chemotherapy. If that scan is cold, you safely avoid a complex, morbid retroperitoneal dissection.

steps.tx: The clinical behavior of **testicular teratoma** depends fundamentally on patient age and developmental status. In prepubertal boys, mature teratoma is a genetically diploid, completely benign neoplasm curable with testis-sparing enucleation. Conversely, in **postpubertal males**, all teratomas (whether mature, immature, or with somatic-type malignancy) derive from germ cell neoplasia in situ, carry the pathognomonic **isochromosome 12p**, possess aggressive metastatic potential, and exhibit profound intrinsic chemo-resistance, requiring complete surgical clearance with **retroperitoneal lymph node dissection**.
steps.say: You must never equate mature teratoma in an adult with the benign dermoid cyst seen in children. In postpubertal men, even histologically mature teratoma carries the cytogenetic hallmark isochromosome 12p and possesses full metastatic capacity. Crucially, mature teratomatous elements do not respond to cytotoxic chemotherapy. Whenever teratoma components are identified, complete surgical extirpation via retroperitoneal lymph node dissection is mandatory to achieve cure.

steps.tx: After receiving cisplatin-based combination chemotherapy for non-seminomatous germ cell tumours, a subset of patients develops **growing teratoma syndrome**. This clinical entity is defined by three strict diagnostic criteria: an enlarging retroperitoneal or visceral mass during or after chemotherapy, paradoxical normalization of previously elevated **serum tumour markers** (alpha-fetoprotein and beta-hCG), and exclusively **benign mature teratoma** on histological resection. Because growing teratoma is resistant to chemotherapy and radiation, complete **surgical resection** is mandatory and curative.
steps.say: Growing teratoma syndrome presents a striking clinical paradox that every oncologist must recognize. While receiving effective cytotoxic therapy, your patient's serum tumor markers drop to completely normal levels, yet follow-up imaging reveals an enlarging retroperitoneal mass. This occurs because chemotherapy eradicates the malignant embryonal and choriocarcinoma cells, leaving behind chemo-resistant mature teratoma that continues growing by mechanical expansion. Immediate complete surgical resection is curative.

vis.alt: Gross specimen of testicular teratoma showing multilocular cystic spaces filled with mucinous and gelatinous fluid.
vis.caption: Testicular teratoma exhibiting multiloculated cystic architecture. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.tx: Pure **testicular choriocarcinoma** produces astronomical elevations of **human chorionic gonadotropin** (beta-hCG, often exceeding 100,000 to 500,000 mIU/mL) while maintaining normal alpha-fetoprotein. Because the shared alpha subunit of hCG exhibits structural homology with thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), extreme circulating beta-hCG concentrations cross-react with and stimulate thyroid follicular cell **TSH receptors**, triggering paraneoplastic **hyperthyroidism** characterized by suppressed serum TSH, elevated free T4, and clinical thyrotoxicosis. Patients frequently present with diffuse bilateral pulmonary cannonball metastases and haemoptysis.
steps.say: Extremely high beta-hCG levels can produce dramatic systemic manifestations beyond the reproductive tract. In pure testicular choriocarcinoma, syncytiotrophoblasts secrete massive amounts of hCG into the circulation. Because hCG shares molecular homology with thyroid-stimulating hormone, it directly stimulates the thyroid gland to release excess thyroid hormones. When a young man presents with severe thyrotoxicosis and diffuse bilateral pulmonary cannonball metastases, measuring serum beta-hCG will immediately clinch the diagnosis.

steps.tx: Representing less than one percent of all **testicular germ cell tumours**, pure choriocarcinoma is the rarest and most lethal subtype. Syncytiotrophoblasts and cytotrophoblasts invade capillaries directly, leading to early, aggressive **hematogenous dissemination** to the lungs, liver, and brain, frequently bypassing the retroperitoneal lymph node filter entirely. Tumours are notorious for extensive internal haemorrhage and **vascular rupture**, precipitating life-threatening retroperitoneal bleeding, intracranial hemorrhage, or massive alveolar hemorrhage upon initiation of cytotoxic chemotherapy (the choriocarcinoma syndrome).
steps.say: Pure choriocarcinoma is the rarest and most ferocious of all testicular germ cell neoplasms, accounting for less than one percent of cases. Unlike other germ cell tumors that spread sequentially through retroperitoneal lymph nodes, choriocarcinoma directly invades vascular channels, seeding the brain, lungs, and liver before the primary tumor is even palpable. Because these tumors are composed of fragile, blood-filled spaces, starting induction chemotherapy requires vigilant intensive care monitoring to manage sudden, catastrophic tumor hemorrhage.
